newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY UNION-WALLABIES FACE POTENTIAL PAY CUT.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-WALLABIES FACE POTENTIAL PAY CUT.

text.p: Australia's top rugby union players are facing a potentially huge pay cut as part of a switch from guaranteed salaries to incentive-based contracts being proposed by the Australian Rugby Union.
ARU chief executive officer John O'Neill said on Tuesday the ruling body would seek to introduce signing-on fees and match payments for tests when current Wallaby player contracts expire.
"There has to be an incentive to play for Australia," O'Neill told Reuters.
About 25 Wallaby players were collectively signed on two or three-year contracts when the code turned professional in 1995. Some of those contracts will expire at the end of the year.
The elite players guaranteed payments ranging between A$200,000 (US$154,000) and A$500,000 per season regardless of performance or injury.
Under the new ARU proposals, a player currently paid A$250,000 might earn a guaranteed A$130,000 with additional payments of about A$10,000 for each test appearance.
Under those terms, he would have to play 12 tests for Australia each year in order to maintain his previous income.
The original contracts, in contrast, took no account of injury, loss of form, or the number of times the individual played for Australia.
At the time of signing in 1995, the players enjoyed a strong bargaining position because they were being sought by the breakaway World Rugby Corporation during its failed takover bid for the sport.
With their control under threat, the ARU agreed to long-term contracts with guaranteed payments -- a position that O'Neill said no longer exists.
"The contracts of 1995 were unique in that players achieved a negotiating position that was simply not repeatable," O'Neill said.
"In the cold light of day, this (the guaranteed payment to players) was commercially unworkable.
"We want to guarantee the top players a handsome reward as a base but to earn significantly higher money, he would have to play for Australia."
But there is expected to be opposition from Australia's three provincial sides, New South Wales, Queensland and Australian Capital Territory (ACT).

The ARU wants to keep the Wallaby squad under contract to the ruling body, while dividing a further A$7 million between the provinces to allow them to complete their squads for the annual Super 12 competition.

Queensland, New South Wales and ACT, however, favour a system in which all the players are contracted to them, with the ARU topping up payments for elite players in addition to test match bonuses, the paper said.
